chapter_theme: A merchant's daughter plays with five balls; one falls in the street before Civakan, she sees him, turns pale and laments that her modesty and restraint are stolen and that desire has no cure, while he, struck by her glance, sits lovesick on her father's step and laments her eyes as Death, and at that moment her father's long-unsold goods sell.

cast.role: the hero, here in the merchants' street of Rajamapuram, unnamed in these verses
the merchant Sagaradattan's daughter, who sees Civakan while playing ball; named in 1975, not in these verses
the merchant, Vimalai's father, whose goods sell when Civakan sits at his step

1953.reading: Five balls rest in the palm of the maiden's hand; as she plays they rise together like bees circling a garland and go up without scattering, and her red-carp eyes and brows travel with their shapes.
1953.nuance: The game is ஐந்து பந்து, five balls kept in the air at once; the verse already makes her eyes follow the balls, the eyes that will soon follow Civakan.

1954.reading: The narrator follows the balls as they hide in her garland and come back to her hand, pass behind her fragrant hair and before her bright face, by a waist thin as thread and at the garland on her crown, and drop back to her fingers.
1954.event: Vimalai keeps the balls moving round her body.

1955.reading: The figures of the game are named, catching and letting go, garlanding, rising in the eight directions, circling in rows, leaping like a peacock, while bees sing, and so the woman plays her five balls.
1955.nuance: The verse is a list of technical moves of the game (கொண்டு நீங்கல், கோதை வேய்தல், எண்டிசையும் ஏற்றல்); some of their exact sense is not recoverable from the words.
1955.event: Vimalai plays through the named figures of the ball game.

1956.reading: As she plays, the saffron on her breasts, the gold powder sprinkled over her and the sandal of the mark on her forehead run down with sweat between her breasts and fall like the rainbow melting.
1956.event: Vimalai sweats as she plays, and her cosmetics run.

1957.reading: With her anklets and girdle-bells laughing, one ball of the gold-garlanded girl leaps out past her jasmine garland, bounds away and falls in the street before the man of the bright spear.
1957.nuance: The narrator gives the ball, not the girl, the move that brings the two together; no one is said to aim it.
1957.event: One of Vimalai's balls flies out and falls in the street before Civakan.

1958.reading: The slender-waisted girl hurries after the fallen ball, her girdle showing, her hair loosening and her garland tumbling onto her breasts, and comes and looks out with wide eyes like a flowering creeper.
1958.event: Vimalai runs out for the ball and looks out into the street.

1959.reading: Crowned with mandara flowers, while drunken bees hum in the gandhara mode, she stands longing for the ball with her lily eyes spread wide, standing like Tiru on the red lotus.
1959.nuance: பந்தார்வம் is longing for the ball; the line keeps her desire on the game a moment before she sees him.
1959.event: Vimalai stands at the doorway looking out.

1960.reading: The creeper on the moonstone terrace, as though fed on cool spray of the Ganga, no sooner sees the young bull than she becomes another, pale as the unopened peerkku flower.
1960.nuance: பீர் (the yellow ridge-gourd flower) is the old sign of the pallor of love; here it comes at first sight, not in separation, which is where the akam poems put it.
1960.event: Vimalai sees Civakan and turns pale.

1961.reading: She says the thief who stole her modesty that never left her, her firm restraint, her beautiful dark skin and grace, the beauty of her eyes and her bangles, is the son of the five-flower-arrowed god come down to earth.
1961.nuance: She lists what a woman's virtue is made of (நாண், நிறை) beside her skin and bangles, as goods a thief has carried off; the loss is put on him, not on her.

1962.reading: She thinks: such is this desire that even if one dies of it, it cannot be told even to one's dearest; it is hard, a hot fire that burns and melts one inside, the one sickness in the world that has no medicine.
1962.nuance: Two silences are joined: the sickness cannot be spoken even to the dearest, and it has no cure; the first is shame (naanam), the second her despair.

claims.claim: desire is the one sickness in the world for which there is no remedy

1963.reading: She says there is no restraint at all where desire that burns like fire exists, and where restraint is whole there is not a kunri seed of desire; the pallor beats it out like a drum, she says, and wilting she stands while desire wide as the roaring sea tosses her.
1963.nuance: The claim is put as an either-or, and the very next verse shows her holding herself with நிறை while desire takes her, so the story does not bear out the rule she states.

claims.claim: restraint and desire cannot dwell together: where one is whole, not a trace of the other remains

1964.reading: Her heart shaken, she stood steadying herself with restraint; but the look of his guileless eyes on her moon-bright face of red-lily eyes gave refuge to desire, and its hot fire took hold of her.
1964.nuance: Whose eyes look at whose face in lines 2-3 is not fixed by the words; the reading here takes the look as his, falling on her face.
1964.event: Vimalai tries to compose herself as Civakan's look falls on her, and desire takes her.

1965.reading: As the flower-eyed girl bent her brow-bows and shot, he asked what medicine there could be for the wound in his scorched heart, looked back at the doe-eyed maiden, and the spear-bearing lord melted and lost his strength.
1965.nuance: His question (என்கொல், line 2) answers her statement two verses back that there is no medicine; the two have now said the same thing without speaking to each other.
1965.event: Civakan, struck by Vimalai's glance, looks back at her and is overcome.

1966.reading: With the fierce fever of desire around him, burning together with this pyre called the body, he could not bear the burning and sat lamenting on the flower-strewn step of the house of the girl's father.
1966.nuance: The body is named a pyre (ஈமம்) that burns with the fire of desire; the image is the renouncer's, used here for a lover. Sitting on the father's step (கடை) is, as 1977 will reveal, the sign that fulfils the girl's horoscope.
1966.event: Civakan sits down, lovesick, at the step of Vimalai's father's shop.

1967.reading: Civakan laments that he does not know who the goddess is that pains his life, she whose hair shames musk and whose carp eyes shame the blue lily, and that there is no one who will come close and bring him word to end his sickness.

1968.reading: He asks whether the womanliness that showed the nature of honeyed lily eyes, and with one look stole all his inner nature that was wide as the sea, knew him already in an earlier birth.
1968.nuance: மேனாள் பிறந்தும் அறியுமோ: the lover reaches for a former birth to explain how one look could take so much; it is asked, not asserted.

1969.reading: He says her dark hair, red mouth, flower eyes, ears and jewelled breasts are Death to the dear life of men, she looks at those who come as guests and leaves them empty bodies, and asks whose daughter this woman of great fortune is and what her name is.

1970.reading: He says that those who named the girl of the strap-bound breasts and bee-swarmed garland called her a woman; had they called her Death, would not garlanded men who wanted their lives have left this sea-girt city?
1970.nuance: போகொடுத்தார் in line 2 is read as பேர் கொடுத்தார், 'those who gave her a name'; the joke turns on that reading.

1971.reading: He says the look she cast with her neck turned, her makara earrings and ear-rolls shining on her moon face, her red mouth and teeth shining and her honeyed hair hanging, appears wherever he looks.

1972.reading: He asks whether her eyes are swords of her bright moon face, or split mango, red lily, blue lily or lotus, long spears, arrows, carp, or long eyes, or Death come full that has begun to kill.
1972.nuance: The list runs through the stock likenesses of eyes and ends on Death that has begun to kill (கொல்வான் தொடங்கின), so the last guess is the one that wins.

1973.reading: As the conqueror sat lamenting and thinking how he could win the girl's beauty, at that very moment the cool Sagaradattan sold, without any loss, six crores' worth of gold-bright goods that had long lain unsold.
1973.nuance: The narrator gives the sale without saying why; the cause, a sign written at Vimalai's birth, is told only by the merchant in 1976-1977.
1973.event: While Civakan sits at his step, the merchant Sagaradattan sells six crores' worth of goods at once.

links.note: Kural 1085 asks whether the maiden's look is Death, an eye or a doe; Civakan asks whether her eyes are swords, mango slices, lilies, lotus, spears, arrows, carp, eyes, or Death come to kill.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet's three-way doubt, the epic's ten guesses show the question turned into a catalogue that closes by choosing Death, where the couplet leaves the look holding all three at once.

gains.a: the verse's list gains a model: it is the couplet's riddle of the look, widened, not a loose string of comparisons
gains.b: the couplet gains a voiced scene, a hero dazed on a merchant's step, in which its question is asked of one particular woman

links.note: Kural 1083: the man never knew Death and now knows it in a woman's warring eyes. Civakan: those who named her called her woman; had they called her Death, men would flee the city.
links.teaches: The pair shows two steps of one discovery: the couplet's man learns that Death has a woman's form, and the epic adds that the name 'woman' hides it, so no one is warned in time.

gains.a: the epic's joke about naming is grounded in the couplet's discovery that Death and a woman are one
gains.b: the couplet's private discovery is made public: if it were known, a whole city would empty

links.note: Vimalai calls desire the one sickness with no medicine; Kural 1102 says the woman who causes the sickness is herself its cure.
links.teaches: Read together they show the two sides of one sickness: to the sufferer who cannot speak of it, it has no cure, while the couplet, spoken from the side of union, finds the cure in the beloved, which the story will supply by marriage.

gains.a: Vimalai's despair is shown to be a stage, not a verdict, since the couplet names the cure her story reaches
gains.b: the couplet's paradox gains a woman's voice, where the Kural gives the man's, and the cure turns out to be needed on both sides

links.note: Kural 1091: her eyes have two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure. Civakan, shot by her brows, asks what medicine there is for the wound and looks back at her.
links.teaches: The couplet's two looks are both hers; the epic gives the second look to him, so the exchange of glances, not one woman's eyes, carries both the wound and the hope of a cure.

gains.a: Civakan's question gains an answer the verse does not state: the cure lies in the look itself
gains.b: the couplet's single-eyed paradox is staged as a mutual exchange in which both lovers fall sick at one glance

links.note: Kural 1180: the town reads the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. Vimalai: her pallor beats out her desire like a drum (பறையாய் அறையும் பசப்பு).
links.teaches: The drum that proclaims a hidden love sits in the eyes in the couplet and in the skin's pallor in the epic, so the pairing shows the body as a whole betraying what restraint tries to keep.

gains.a: Vimalai's drum image is placed in an old line of thought about love that cannot be hidden
gains.b: the couplet's eyes gain a partner: the skin too announces the secret, and at first sight, not only after long love

links.note: In 1963 Vimalai holds that restraint and desire cannot coexist; in 1964 she stands steadying herself with restraint while desire seizes her.
links.teaches: Her rule that restraint and desire exclude each other is contradicted at once by the story, which shows a woman holding restraint and burning with desire at the same moment.

links.note: Kuruntokai 40's lover marvels that strangers' hearts mingled like rain and red earth; Civakan asks whether the woman who took his heart with one look knew him in a former birth.
links.teaches: Facing the same mystery of a stranger's sudden hold, the Sangam lover lets the merging stand without cause, while the Jain epic's hero reaches for a past birth, so the pair shows rebirth entering the love lyric as an explanation.

gains.a: Civakan's question is seen as a choice: the old poetry had answered the same wonder without any former life
gains.b: the Kuruntokai's uncaused union is set against a later frame in which love itself has a karmic past

links.note: Pattinattar lists the body as a feast thrown to the pyre's fire (ஈமக் கனல்) and a leaf scorched in the fire of desire (காமக் கனல்); Civakan's body, called a pyre (ஈமம்), burns in desire's fever (காமக் கடுநோய்க் கனல்).
links.teaches: The same pairing of pyre and desire's fire is a reason to renounce the body in Pattinattar and a lover's complaint in the epic, so the image does not carry its lesson with it: the hero who will one day renounce here uses it only to say how much he burns.

gains.a: the epic's hyperbole is shown to borrow the renouncer's figure, which the Cintamani will later take back seriously when Civakan renounces
gains.b: Pattinattar's figure is seen to be older than his use of it: in love poetry the pyre-body burns without teaching contempt for the body

links.note: In 1973 Sagaradattan suddenly sells six crores of goods while Civakan sits at his step; in 1977 the merchant tells that it was written at Vimalai's birth that goods would sell when her destined husband sat at his shop.
links.teaches: The unexplained sale is the fulfilment of a birth-sign told only afterwards, so the narrator lets the reader see the sign come true before learning that it was one.

links.note: In 1948 the city's women ask whether he is Murugan or the five-arrowed Kama; in 1961 Vimalai decides he is the son of the five-flower-arrowed god come down to earth.
links.teaches: The question the crowd of women asked and left open is answered by the one woman who will marry him, and for her the answer costs her modesty and restraint.

source_issues: 1955 line 3 மணிடி லம்வ ரப்புடைத்தன் is garbled as printed (likely மண்டிலம், 'a circle'); 1955, 1957, 1958 and 1970 were printed in 8 half-lines and joined.
1958 line 2 கின்னெகிழ்ந்து is likely a misprint (perhaps கண் or கச்சு நெகிழ்ந்து); the sense 'loosening' is clear, the noun is not.
1970 line 2 போகொடுத்தார் is likely a misprint of பேர்கொடுத்தார்; line 4 விந்நகரை நீத்திட டொழியாரோ has a doubled syllable.
1971 line 2 முகத்திலங்க்ச் carries a stray virama (for முகத்திலங்கச்).
1960 lines 1-2 (நீர்தங்கு திங்கண் மணிநீணிலம், கங்கைத் திருநீர்த் துவலை மாந்தி) are obscure as divided; the moonstone-terrace reading is a guess.
